facts_full_text:
**Given:** Full AC and the supplied embedding of the closed product collar.

[A1] Full AC, including the dependent countable choices used below. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] Under AC a continuous injective map between open three-dimensional coordinate domains is open. Its local restrictions give the same conclusion between boundaryless three-manifolds. [[thm-invariance-of-domain]]

[F2] An embedded two-sphere in $S^3$ has two complementary open path components with that sphere as common boundary. [[thm-jordan-brouwer-separation]]

[F3] Under AC, Alexander duality identifies $\widetilde H_0(S^3\setminus K;\mathbb Z)$ with $\widetilde H^2(K;\mathbb Z)$ for a nonempty proper compact weakly locally contractible subset $K$. Zero-th homology is the free abelian group on path components. [[thm-alexander-duality-for-compact-locally-contractible-subsets-of-a-sphere]] [[prop-zero-th-singular-homology-is-free-on-path-components]]

proof_steps.full_text: We first prove a finite-fiber image fact. Let $Q$ be a parametrized topological closed three-ball and $f:Q\to S^3$ continuous, with finitely many nonsingleton fibers, all contained in $\operatorname{Int}Q$. Its boundary is mapped injectively and hence homeomorphically onto an embedded sphere $L$: a continuous bijection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space has continuous inverse, since images of closed subsets are compact and closed. No interior point maps to $L$, as that would give a nonsingleton fiber meeting the boundary. Thus the connected image $f(\operatorname{Int}Q)$ lies in one component $D$ of $S^3\setminus L$. Let $P$ be the finite set of exceptional image points. Their preimages form a compact subset of $\operatorname{Int}Q$, so a thin inner collar of the domain boundary contains a point outside those fibers. Its image is a nonexceptional point of $D$. At every such image point the unique preimage has a coordinate neighborhood disjoint from those finitely many fibers. On that neighborhood $f$ is injective, and [F1] makes its image open in $S^3$. Therefore $f(Q)\cap(D\setminus P)$ is nonempty and both open and closed in $D\setminus P$. Deleting finitely many points from the connected open three-manifold $D$ preserves path connectedness: for a path, take disjoint small closed coordinate balls about the unwanted points, and replace its segment from first to last encounter with a still smaller sphere by a path on that sphere. Finitely many replacements avoid all the points. Hence $D\setminus P\subset f(Q)$. It is dense in $D$, while $f(Q)$ is closed, so $f(Q)=D\cup L$ and $f(\operatorname{Int}Q)=D$. [A1, F1, F2, given, construct]

Return to the supplied collar. Set $L_\pm=h(S^2\times\{\pm1\})$. Their union has exactly three complementary components. Indeed it is homeomorphic to a disjoint union of two ordinary two-spheres, and therefore has $H^2=\mathbb Z^2$: [F3] applied to the standard equator computes $H^2(S^2)=\mathbb Z$ from its explicit two hemispheres, and every singular simplex in a two-component disjoint union lies in one component, so its cochain complex is the direct product of the two complexes. [F3] now gives reduced $H_0=\mathbb Z^2$ for the complement of $L_+\cup L_-$. Its open path components have the basis-difference description of [F3], so there are exactly three: a finite set of $r$ distinct nonbase components gives $r$ independent integral vectors, and a subgroup of $\mathbb Z^2$ has at most two independent vectors, as is seen over $\mathbb Q$; the group cannot be generated by fewer than two. The open image $h(S^2\times(-1,1))$ is one whole component, since [F1] makes it open and compactness of the full collar makes it closed relative to this complement. It is connected. The component outside $L_+$ not containing this middle region is disjoint from the whole collar, as the latter's part below $L_+$ is connected and avoids $L_+$. Similarly there is an outside component for $L_-$. They are distinct. Otherwise both spheres' common-boundary property in [F2] would put $L_-$ in the closure of that outside $L_+$ component, whereas the entire compact $L_-$ lies in its other open component. Denote their closures by $A,B$ respectively. They and the full collar exhaust $S^3$, meet the collar exactly in $L_+,L_-$, and are disjoint from one another. [A1, F1, F2, F3, given, construct, algebra]

Call a nonempty compact set $M$ cellular in a three-manifold if it is the intersection of parametrized closed three-balls $Q_j$ with $Q_{j+1}\subset\operatorname{Int}Q_j$. If $M\subset\operatorname{Int}Q$ is cellular there and has at least two points, it can be collapsed by a continuous surjection $c:Q	o Q$ fixed on $\partial Q$ with precisely $M$ as its only nonsingleton fiber. Here is the construction. Discard finitely many witnessing balls so all lie in $\operatorname{Int}Q$, and put $Q_0=Q$. Starting with $c_0=\mathrm{id}$, construct homeomorphisms $c_j:Q	o Q$, fixed on $\partial Q$, equal to $c_{j-1}$ outside $Q_{j-1}$ and with $\operatorname{diam}c_j(Q_j)<2^{-j}$ in the metric of a fixed parameter of $Q$. In the parameter of the current ball $c_{j-1}(Q_{j-1})$, the compact set $c_{j-1}(Q_j)$ lies in a smaller concentric ball. A strictly increasing piecewise linear change of radial coordinate, fixed at radius one and at zero, takes that smaller ball into an arbitrarily small central ball. Extend this radial homeomorphism by the identity outside the current ball, and compose with $c_{j-1}$. Uniform continuity of its supplied parameter gives the required metric diameter. Later maps preserve the set $B_j=c_j(Q_j)$ and agree with $c_j$ off $Q_j$. Conversely, if a continuous map $f:Q\to S^3$ from a parametrized three-ball has just one nonsingleton fiber $M\subset\operatorname{Int}Q$, then $M$ is cellular in $\operatorname{Int}Q$. By step 1.1 its image is a proper closed domain $F=D\cup L$, and $p=f(M)$ lies in $D$. Given any open neighborhood $U$ of $M$ inside $Q$, it is saturated for $f$, since every other fiber is a singleton. Compactness makes $f$ a closed quotient map onto $F$, so $f(U)$ is open relative to $F$. Choose a small open neighborhood $O$ of $p$ in $S^3$ with closure in $D\cap f(U)$. There is an ambient homeomorphism $a:S^3\to S^3$ taking $F$ into $O$ and fixed on a neighborhood $V$ of $p$. To see this explicitly, choose a point outside the compact proper $F$ and use its stereographic chart, centered at $p$. Then $F$ lies in a finite-radius ball. A strictly increasing radial homeomorphism, equal to the identity at sufficiently small radii and at sufficiently large radii, compresses that finite-radius ball into a small ball about $p$ contained in $O$; extend it by the identity at infinity. Define $g(x)=x$ on $M$, and on $Q\setminus M$ define $g(x)$ as the unique preimage of $a(f(x))$ under $f$. This is defined because $a(F)\subset f(U)$, and $a(f(x))\ne p$ when $x\notin M$. Off $M$ it is a conjugation of homeomorphisms: the restriction of $f$ away from its exceptional fiber and value is a homeomorphism, as follows locally from its closed quotient property. On the neighborhood $f^{-1}(V)$ the map $g$ is the identity, so it is continuous at $M$ as well. It is injective, including on $M$, and its compact image is therefore a parametrized three-ball $g(Q)\subset U$. Since it fixes a neighborhood of $M$, that ball contains $M$ in its interior. Recursively use $U=\operatorname{Int}Q$ first, and then the intersection of the preceding ball's interior with the metric $2^{-j}$-neighborhood of $M$. [A1] supplies the resulting sequence and its parameters. Its intersection is exactly $M$, proving cellularity. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, construct]

If a continuous surjection $f:S^3\to S^3$ has precisely two nonsingleton fibers $A,B$, then both are cellular. They are disjoint compact sets. There is a point outside their union: otherwise their two nonempty disjoint closed sets would disconnect $S^3$. In its stereographic chart take a round closed ball $Q$ containing $A\cup B$ in its interior. Step 1.1 gives $f(Q)=D\cup L=F$. The distinct points $a=f(A)$ and $b=f(B)$ belong to $D$. Choose a small open neighborhood $O\subset D$ of $a$ not containing $b$. The radial construction in step 2.2 gives a homeomorphism $u$ of $S^3$ taking $F$ into $O$ and fixed near $a$. Define $g:Q\to Q$ to be the identity on $A$ and the unique preimage of $u(f(x))$ otherwise. These preimages exist in $Q$, since $u(F)\subset D=f(\operatorname{Int}Q)$, and are unique except when the target is $a$ or $b$; $b$ is excluded by $O$, and $a$ occurs only for $x\in A$. On a neighborhood of $A$ the map is the identity, so it is continuous there; elsewhere continuity of the inverse off the exceptional fibers follows from the closed quotient property, as in step 2.2. Exactly $B$ is collapsed: the points of $B$ have common target $u(b)\notin\{a,b\}$, all other points outside $A$ remain distinguished, and no such image enters $A$. Hence step 2.2 applied to $g$ proves that $B$ is cellular. Interchange $A,B$ to prove the same for $A$. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.2, construct]

We also record the quotient repair with the boundary parameter intact. Let $C$ be a compact Hausdorff space, $R$ a parametrized closed three-ball, and $f:C\to R$ a continuous surjection with only one nonsingleton fiber $M$. Suppose $M$ lies in a parametrized ball $Q\subset C$ whose interior is open in $C$, and is cellular there. Assume $f$ is injective on $C\setminus M$ and maps a specified outside boundary of $C$ homeomorphically to $\partial R$, away from $Q$. The map $c:Q\to Q$ of step 2.1 extends by the identity to a continuous surjection $c':C\to C$, since it fixes $\partial Q$. It is a quotient map by compactness and Hausdorffness and has exactly the same fibers as $f$. Thus there is a unique induced continuous bijection $H:C\to R$ with $Hc'=f$. It is a homeomorphism by compactness. On the outside boundary, $c'$ is the identity, so $H$ has the exact boundary value of $f$. No inverse of the noninjective collapse map was asserted. [A1, step 2.1, construct]

Define $f:S^3\to S^3\subset\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ by collapsing $A$ to the north pole and $B$ to the south pole, and by $f(h(s,t))=(\sqrt{1-t^2}\,s,t)$ on the collar. The definitions agree on the two end spheres. All three pieces are compact and cover the domain, so this is continuous by finite closed pasting. It is surjective and its only nonsingleton fibers are $A,B$. Step 3.1 makes them cellular. The two closed sets $C_+=A\cup h(S^2\times[0,1])$ and $C_-=B\cup h(S^2\times[-1,0])$ cover $S^3$ and meet exactly in $S$. Their complements of $S$ are disjoint nonempty open connected sets: each is the closure of its outer connected domain, with its attaching sphere and a connected half collar added, while removing only the opposite middle end; this union remains connected because the attaching sphere lies in the closure of the outer domain and meets the half collar. Thus these are precisely the two components of $S^3\setminus S$, also by [F2]. The compact $A$ lies in the open component on the positive side; therefore its cellular witnessing balls eventually lie wholly inside that component. If none did, nested compactness would give a point of their intersection outside that open component, contradicting their intersection being $A$. The same holds for $B$ on the negative side. [A1, F1, F2, step 3.1, step 1.2, construct]

The restrictions $f:C_\pm\to R_\pm$, where $R_\pm$ are the two standard closed hemispheres, now satisfy step 3.2. Choose a sufficiently late cellular witnessing ball for $A$ or $B$ entirely in the open side; its interior is open in $S^3$ by [F1] applied to its ball parameter. Tail witnesses give cellularity within it. The quotient repair supplies homeomorphisms $H_\pm:C_\pm\to R_\pm$ with exact boundary value $H_\pm(h(s,0))=(s,0)$. The standard hemisphere parameters $x\mapsto(x,\pm\sqrt{1-|x|^2})$ are homeomorphisms from $D^3$ to $R_\pm$ and have boundary value $(s,0)$. Compose them with $H_\pm^{-1}$ to obtain the claimed $b_\pm$. The full AC hypothesis has been used honestly in the stated topological suppliers and cellular witness recursion. Nothing in this construction gives a PL ball parameter or a smooth ambient isotopy; it does not supply the missing choice-free TOP-to-PL Moise bridge. [A1, F1, step 3.2, step 4.1, construct] ∎
